name: PIQA
description: Physical Interaction: Question Answering (PIQA) is a benchmark dataset for physical commonsense reasoning in natural language. Given a physical goal expressed in natural language and two possible solutions, a model or human must choose the most appropriate solution, of which exactly one is correct.
creator: Yonatan Bisk; Rowan Zellers; Ronan Le Bras; Jianfeng Gao; Yejin Choi
citeAs: Bisk, Yonatan; Zellers, Rowan; Le Bras, Ronan; Gao, Jianfeng; Choi, Yejin. PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language. 2020.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected as goal-solution pairs using how-to instructions as a scaffold. Annotators were prompted with links to instructables.com, asked to glance at the instructions of an instructable, and use it to inspire construction of two component tasks. They articulated a physical goal, a valid solution, and a permutation of their own solution that makes it invalid. Annotators were seeded with instructables drawn from six categories: costume, outside, craft, home, food, and workshop. Additional qualification HITs were run prior to the main annotation stage and validation was performed afterwards by other annotators for correctness.
rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Prompts were derived from instructables.com, a crowdsourced collection of instructions for building, crafting, baking, or manipulating objects using everyday materials.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was further cleaned of basic artifacts using the AFLite algorithm. AFLite was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples by discarding instances whose feature representations were highly indicative of the target label. The train, development, and test folds were automatically produced by AFLite.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Examples with low agreement were removed during validation. This often removed correct examples that required expert-level domain knowledge. The dataset was cleaned using AFLite to reduce annotation artifacts and spurious biases. Goals were tokenized by Spacy, and examples were collected in English.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were asked to provide a physical goal, a valid solution, and a trick: a permutation of their own solution that sounds reasonable but is wrong, often due to a subtle misunderstanding of preconditions or physics. They were prompted with instructables to encourage creative, less prototypical uses of everyday objects. A qualification HIT containing well-constructed and underspecified goal-solution pairs was used; annotators had to identify which were well formed with greater than 80% accuracy to participate in the main HIT. Data was collected in batches of several thousand triples and validated by other annotators for correctness. During validation, examples with low agreement were removed. Human performance was calculated by majority vote, and annotators for human evaluation were chosen if they achieved at least 90% on the qualification HIT.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: During validation, examples with low agreement were removed. Human performance was calculated by majority vote. The interface included a diff button highlighting where the two solutions differ, which improved annotator accuracy and speed substantially.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors position PIQA as a benchmark to advance language representations that capture physical commonsense knowledge useful beyond NLP, including for robots that interact with the world and understand natural language. They argue that learning about the world from language alone is limiting and that knowledge should eventually be learned from interaction with the world.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly discusses reporting bias: when thinking about how to achieve a goal, people are drawn to prototypical solutions and common tools such as forks, knives, hammers, and drills, while rarely considering many other everyday objects. The dataset was designed to flatten the distribution of referenced objects by prompting annotators with instructables, and AFLite was used to remove stylistic artifacts and trivial examples.
rai:dataLimitations: Some examples judged as mistakes were actually correct but required a web search to verify. Examples requiring expert-level domain knowledge were removed because they should not fall under commonsense. The authors note that future systems may match humans on the dataset by finding large in-domain data and fine-tuning heavily, but argue that this is not the intended point of the benchmark.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is introduced as a benchmark for evaluating and studying physical commonsense understanding in natural language models. It contains over 16,000 training QA pairs with approximately 2K development and approximately 3K test examples, indicating use for training, development/validation, and testing.
